The year was 1954, and the lighthouse stood on Blackrock Point, a slab of granite three hundred feet above the Atlantic. For forty-one years, since 1913, it had been kept by Elias Thorne. His wife, Martha, had died in 1949, and since then the only sounds in the tower were the sweep of the lens, the groan of the gallery rail in the wind, and the radio, which Elias kept on for the news and the ships.

On a Tuesday in November, the sea was grey and the sky lower still. Elias was down below, scrubbing the brass of the lantern room, when the radio crackled.

"...vessel in distress. Position off Blackrock. Three hundred miles east of here. Requesting assistance."

Elias grabbed his coat. He knew that radio code. It was not for him, but he knew it anyway, from the navy days before the light.

He climbed the three hundred and seventy-two steps. The great Fresnel lens turned, a slow, golden eye cutting through the rain. He checked the fuel, the wick, the clockwork, and wrote in the log: *14:10. Lens clean. Fuel normal. Weather: poor.*

Then he went back down. The radio was still crackling. He listened. A ship was going down three hundred miles east of Blackrock, and the nearest coast guard cutter was hours away. Elias thought about the men on that ship, and then he thought about the log.

The log was the one thing in the lighthouse that had to be true. If he wrote in the log that the weather was clear, and a ship went down because someone believed the log, the log had killed them. He would never write anything in it that he did not believe.

That evening, after the radio had gone quiet and the cutter had not yet answered, Elias sat at his desk. He had a bottle of ink and a ream of paper. He wrote:

*Blackrock Point, 1954. This lighthouse has stood here since 1913. I am Elias Thorne, keeper since 1913. The lens works. The fuel is good. The log is true. If you are reading this, the light worked.*

He rolled the paper tight, tied it with string, and put it in a glass bottle. He did not know why. He did not know who would read it. He knew only that the light had done its work, and someone ought to know.

He carried the bottle to the gallery. The wind was howling now. He thought of the ship, and of the men who might be in the water. Then he thought of the log, and of the next keeper, who would come in 1998, or 2024, or never.

He threw the bottle into the sea.

The year was 1998. A young man named Daniel Ruiz stood on the same gallery, holding a glass bottle. He had been walking the coast for three days, looking for glass that might have come from the old tower. He was not a keeper. He was a student of history, and he wanted to know what the keepers had written down.

The bottle was heavy. Inside was a roll of paper, yellow with age. Daniel unrolled it carefully in the shelter of the gallery.

*Blackrock Point, 1954. This lighthouse has stood here since 1913. I am Elias Thorne, keeper since 1913. The lens works. The fuel is good. The log is true. If you are reading this, the light worked.*

Daniel read it three times. Outside, the sea was grey and the sky was lower still. He thought about the ship that had gone down three hundred miles east of Blackrock in 1954, and about the cutter that had not come in time. He thought about the man who had thrown the bottle into the sea that night, and about the log that had told the truth.

Daniel wrote in his notebook:

*Blackrock Point, 1998. Found a bottle in the sea. Message from Elias Thorne, keeper 1913 to 1954. The light worked. The log was true.*

The year was 2024. The lighthouse was automated. No one lived in the tower. A woman named Sarah Okafor stood on the gallery, checking the sensors. She was a technician, not a keeper. She had come to replace the old lens with a modern one.

In her pocket she had a notebook. In it was a copy of the message Daniel had found in 1998.

She read it again. Then she looked at the lens, turning slowly, golden, still.

She wrote in her notebook:

*Blackrock Point, 2024. Sensor check. Lens still turns. Fuel: electric. Log: digital. Elias Thorne was right. The light worked.*

She put the notebook back in her pocket. She did not change the sensor readings. She did not change the log. She wrote down what she saw.

Outside, the sea was grey and the sky was lower still.

The year was 2050. The lighthouse was dark. The lens had been removed in 2024, and the tower stood empty. A man named James Thorne stood on the gallery. He was Elias's great-grandson. He did not know why he had come.

In his hand he held a bottle. Inside was a roll of paper, yellow with age.

*Blackrock Point, 2024. Sensor check. Lens still turns. Fuel: electric. Log: digital. Elias Thorne was right. The light worked.*

James read it twice. Then he looked at the dark tower.

He wrote in his notebook:

*Blackrock Point, 2050. Found a message in a bottle. From Sarah Okafor, 2024. From Daniel Ruiz, 1998. From Elias Thorne, 1954. The light worked.*

He put the bottle back in his pocket. He did not light the tower. He did not change the log. He wrote down what he saw.

Outside, the sea was grey and the sky was lower still.

The year was 2076. The lighthouse was gone. The tower had fallen in 2050, and the sea had taken the granite. A woman named Martha Thorne stood on the shore. She was Elias's great-great-granddaughter. She did not know why she had come.

In her hand she held a piece of paper, yellow with age.

*Blackrock Point, 2050. Found a message in a bottle. From Sarah Okafor, 2024. From Daniel Ruiz, 1998. From Elias Thorne, 1954. The light worked.*

Martha read it three times. Then she looked at the sea.

She wrote in her notebook:

*Blackrock Point, 2076. The tower is gone. The light worked. Elias Thorne was right.*

She put the paper in her pocket. She did not change the log. She wrote down what she saw.

Outside, the sea was grey and the sky was lower still.

The year was 2100. The sea had taken the shore. A man named Elias Thorne stood on the cliff. He was not a keeper. He was a man.

In his hand he held a bottle. Inside was a roll of paper, yellow with age.

*Blackrock Point, 2076. The tower is gone. The light worked. Elias Thorne was right.*

Elias read it twice. Then he looked at the sea.

He wrote in his notebook:

*Blackrock Point, 2100. Found a message in a bottle. From Martha Thorne, 2076. From James Thorne, 2050. From Sarah Okafor, 2024. From Daniel Ruiz, 1998. From Elias Thorne, 1954. The light worked.*

He put the bottle in the sea.

Outside, the sea was grey and the sky was lower still.

The log was true. The light had worked. The message had been passed on, from keeper to keeper, from keeper to student, from student to technician, from technician to grandson, from grandson to great-great-granddaughter, from great-great-granddaughter to a man named Elias.

The year was 2100. The sea was grey. The sky was lower still.

The message was still being written.

The end.

The year was 1954, and the name of the keeper was Elias Thorne. He had kept the Blackwood Point Lighthouse for nineteen years, ever since his father retired and left him the job and the small stone house that clung to the cliff like a barnacle.

On a Tuesday in November, the weather was bad enough to make even the gulls stay on the rocks. Elias was down in the cellar, sorting through old jars of preserved lemons, when his boot kicked something that didn't sound like glass or stone. It was a bottle, corked and sealed with wax, half-buried in the damp earth near the foundation. He pulled it out. The glass was green and thick, and something was written on a scrap of paper inside.

He took it up to the kitchen and sat by the stove to read it. The handwriting was neat and old-fashioned, written in ink that had faded to brown.

*To whoever finds this: I am Captain Alistair Reed of the SS Meridian. On the night of March 14, 1902, our ship went down three miles east of Blackwood Point. I was thrown into the water and swam for hours. The light did not turn that night. I do not know why. I do not know if anyone saw us. If this reaches you, please tell my family in Liverpool that I lived long enough to be lost, and that I am not afraid of the sea. A. Reed, 1902.*

Elias read it twice. The date on the clock on the wall said 11:40 PM. He looked at the tower above him, where the great lens turned steadily in its bath of oil, throwing its beam out across the dark water every ten seconds.

He went to the logbook on the desk. The last entry had been made on November 1st, and it was his own handwriting, dated 1954. He opened the back cover and found a page that had been torn out. He remembered now, vaguely, his father saying something about a gap in the records around 1902.

He wrote at the top of the new page: *November, 1954. Found this bottle in the cellar of the lighthouse.*

Then he copied the message out, word for word, so that no one would ever have to wonder what had been written inside.

The next morning he took the bottle to the post office in the nearby village of Harrow's Bay. The postmaster, a man named Mr. Hallett, read the message and frowned.

"Liverpool," he said. "That's a long way to send a note about a man who died over fifty years ago."

"I don't think he died," Elias said. "I think he was lost. And he wanted someone to know."

So Mr. Hallett wrote the address on a piece of paper and sealed it in an envelope. Elias gave him the bottle to keep, because he suspected it was worth more than the letter.

The letter went out on Wednesday. Elias went back to his work. He trimmed the wicks, polished the lens, and walked the cliff path to make sure no one was standing too close to the edge.

On Friday, a letter came back. It was from a woman in Liverpool. Her name was Margaret Reed, and she said she was the granddaughter of Captain Alistair Reed. She said that his family had always wondered what had happened to him, and that no one had ever told them.

She wrote that she would come to Blackwood Point in the spring, if the keeper would meet her.

Elias wrote back and told her he would be there.

In the spring, the weather was good enough for the gulls to come out again. Margaret Reed came on a train and then a bus, and she walked up the cliff path with Elias. She was older than he expected, with grey hair and a face that had seen a lot of walking.

She stood at the base of the tower and looked up at the light.

"He wrote that the light did not turn that night," she said.

"No," Elias said. "But it turned the next night. And every night since."

She took out a photograph from her bag. It was a man in a captain's uniform, standing on the deck of a ship. He was smiling, and he looked like a man who was not afraid of the sea.

"Thank you," she said. "For telling me."

"You can thank the light," Elias said. "It never stopped turning."

She stayed for lunch, and they ate at the kitchen table with the bottle sitting on the shelf behind them. When she left, she took a copy of the message with her. Elias kept the original in the logbook.

That evening, Elias wrote in the logbook: *November 1954. Message delivered. Captain Reed's family knows he was lost, and that he was not afraid.*

He closed the book and went up to the tower. The lens turned, and the beam swept across the water, and he watched it go all the way to the horizon.

The bottle was still in the cellar, and the message was still in the logbook, and the light still turned every ten seconds, no matter what the weather was like.

In the spring, the weather was good enough for the gulls to come out again. Margaret Reed came on a train and then a bus, and she walked up the cliff path with Elias. She was older than he expected, with grey hair and a face that had seen a lot of walking.

She stood at the base of the tower and looked up at the light.

"He wrote that the light did not turn that night," she said.

"No," Elias said. "But it turned the next night. And every night since."

She took out a photograph from her bag. It was a man in a captain's uniform, standing on the deck of a ship. He was smiling, and he looked like a man who was not afraid of the sea.

"Thank you," she said. "For telling me."

"You can thank the light," Elias said. "It never stopped turning."

She stayed for lunch, and they ate at the kitchen table with the bottle sitting on the shelf behind them. When she left, she took a copy of the message with her. Elias kept the original in the logbook.

That evening, Elias wrote in the logbook: *November 1954. Message delivered. Captain Reed's family knows he was lost, and that he was not afraid.*

He closed the book and went up to the tower. The lens turned, and the beam swept across the water, and he watched it go all the way to the horizon.

The year was 1954, and the name of the keeper was Elias Thorne. He had kept the Blackwood Point Lighthouse for nineteen years, and he would keep it for many more. The bottle was still in the cellar, and the message was still in the logbook, and the light still turned every ten seconds, no matter what the weather was like.

The end.
